title: 1. Start here: one useful problem
body:
Welcome. This is a free, written course. There are no videos to wait for, and none are planned. Read, try, check your result and move at your own pace. AI tools and hosting may have separate costs.

Your goal is a small local prototype you can understand and test. Completing this course does not make an app ready for real customers or sensitive data.

Companion guide: https://agenticbuilders.brainit.site/
Read “What an agent is” and “Things worth building.” Time estimates are illustrations, not deadlines. Check current provider documentation for tool requirements and prices.

TRY IT
Choose one repeated job: following up estimates, keeping job notes, tracking stock or booking visits. Use fictional examples.

Write four lines:
• Today I keep track of …
• The person using this will be …
• Version one only needs to …
• It will not handle … yet.

Example: “I track garden visits in a notebook. Only I use it. I need a property name, date, job note and done checkbox. No payments, customer login or automatic messages.”

CHECK YOUR PROGRESS
Can you describe version one in two sentences without adding “and also”? Remove one feature if needed. Save extra ideas for later. Mark this lesson done when you have your four-line brief.

Quick check: Is the biggest app the best first project? No. A small useful workflow is easier to finish and test.

title: 2. Understand the agent and set boundaries
body:
An AI coding agent can inspect files, edit code and run checks, depending on its permissions. You supply the business knowledge. Its confidence is not proof that its work is correct.

Read: https://agenticbuilders.brainit.site/#loop

THE LOOP
Describe → agree a small plan → build → inspect and test → give feedback. Repeat. Ask what changed and how it was checked.

PREPARE
Choose an agent you already have access to, such as Claude Code or Codex. Follow its current official installation instructions. Do not buy a plan just to read this course; you can do the planning exercises first.

Create a new empty practice folder and open it in the agent. Keep real business files elsewhere. Use fictional names and records. Review permission prompts.

FIRST MESSAGE
“I want a small local practice app. Ask about my workflow before building. Use fictional data. Explain the plan and how to test it. Ask before spending money, publishing, sending messages, deleting existing work or connecting real customer data.”

This states your boundary; it is not a technical guarantee. Review the proposed actions yourself.

CHECK YOUR PROGRESS
Identify the practice folder, explain what the agent may do and name an action needing your approval. Mark done when these are clear.

Quick check: Is an agent’s claim that a test passed enough? No. Ask which test, then try the important workflow yourself.

title: 3. Turn your workflow into a small plan
body:
Read the guide’s examples:
https://agenticbuilders.brainit.site/#answers

Good answers describe the work. “A booking system” leaves out the details. “I book garden visits by phone and need the property, date, job and status” gives the agent something concrete.

ANSWER THESE
1. Who uses version one?
2. What must it remember?
3. What are the three most important actions?
4. Who needs access? Keep this practice version local and single-user.
5. What is outside version one?
6. What would prove it is useful?

BrainIT’s start-an-app skill is optional. Inspect its source and instructions before installing it. A skill guides the agent; it is not a security boundary.
https://agenticbuilders.brainit.site/#skill

ASK FOR A READ-BACK
“Summarize the first version before changing files. List its fields, screens and actions, and what we are leaving out. Give me five checks I can perform. Keep it local with fictional data.”

Example checks: add a visit; find it; change its date; mark it complete; restart and confirm it remains saved.

CHECK YOUR PROGRESS
Compare the plan with your brief. Correct assumptions now. Save the agreed plan. Mark done when the plan and checks describe the same small app.

Quick check: Who decides what the business needs? You. Asking for a technical recommendation is fine; your business requirements still need your input.

title: 4. Build, inspect and give useful feedback
body:
Let the agent build the agreed version in small steps. Ask how to start and stop the app and for the exact local address. The start command depends on the project.

TRY IT
With fictional records, run your five checks. Also try an empty form, a missing required value and a long note. Record the expected result, actual result and steps.

Useful feedback:
“When I change the visit date and reopen the record, the old date returns. I expected the new one to remain. Here are the steps.”

Ask:
“Find the cause, make the smallest appropriate fix and repeat the failing check. Tell me what you verified and what is still uncertain.”

SAVE A CHECKPOINT
Ask for a local Git checkpoint of the working source. Keep secrets, customer data and database files out of source control. A source checkpoint and a database backup serve different purposes.

Troubleshooting examples:
https://agenticbuilders.brainit.site/#wrong

CHECK YOUR PROGRESS
All five workflow checks pass with fictional data. You can restart the app yourself and locate its source checkpoint. Fix failed checks before marking done.

Quick check: Add ten features while saving is broken? No. Fix and recheck the basic workflow first.

title: 5. The prototype is not the product
body:
A prototype can appear quickly. Making it dependable for real users takes further work. A polished screen does not prove privacy, working backups or correct permissions.

Read: https://agenticbuilders.brainit.site/#after

BEFORE REAL USE
• Decide who may see and change each record.
• Test permissions using separate accounts when accounts are needed.
• Keep secrets out of browser code and Git.
• Validate input and test failures.
• Back up data and practice restoring a separate copy.
• Decide who handles maintenance.
• Check hosting terms, limits and costs before publishing.

A security scanner helps find issues; it is not a certificate of safety. Investigate findings instead of dismissing them because the app is new. Get appropriate specialist review before handling sensitive or regulated data.

PRACTICE
Back up fictional test data. Restore it into a separate test location. Verify a known record. Never practice your first restore over your only live database.

Write a readiness note with three lists: Verified, Not tested yet, Needs help. Name who will handle each unresolved item.

CHECK YOUR PROGRESS
Explain why a prototype is not a public launch. Save the readiness note and a demonstrated restore result. Staying local is a valid choice.

Quick check: Does an unadvertised public link protect customer data? No. A link is not access control.

title: 6. Choose your next useful step
body:
You now have a brief, plan, test results and readiness note. These are valuable even if you never publish the app.

CHOOSE A PATH
Keep learning: improve one small part, then repeat the checks.
Get a review: have a trusted developer inspect the actual app, data needs and access controls.
Stop here: use the prototype and notes as a specification for someone else.

YOUR HAND-OVER CHECKLIST
• What problem does this solve, and for whom?
• Where are the source files and saved records?
• How do I start and stop it?
• What has been tested, and what has not?
• How do I back up and restore it?
• Who owns the accounts and handles maintenance?
• What is the next small change and how will I check it?

When asking for help, share the symptom, reproduction steps and expected result. Remove passwords, keys and private customer information. Do not post a live database in the community.

Optional help: BrainIT Consulting offers reviews, training, projects and help getting unstuck, in northeast Georgia and online across the USA.
https://brainit.site/
You do not need to buy anything from BrainIT to finish.

CHECK YOUR PROGRESS
Save your hand-over checklist and take the final quiz. No timer, no penalty for trying again. Your result is a workflow you can explain and test.

title: 7. Final self-check quiz and answers
body:
Write your answers before reading the key. One point per correct answer. This is a self-check, not certification or a security assessment. Answers are not submitted or automatically graded.

1. Best first project?
A. Every process at once.
B. One repeated task with a small set of fields.

2. Practice using:
A. Fictional data in a separate folder.
B. Your only live customer database.

3. The agent says “done.” Next?
A. Publish.
B. Ask what it tested and run your checks.

4. Better feedback?
A. “Make it better.”
B. “The saved date changes back; here are the steps.”

5. Does Git replace a database backup?
A. Yes.
B. No.

6. A security finding appears. You:
A. Investigate and decide what must be fixed.
B. Ignore it because the app is new.

7. Is an unadvertised public link access control?
A. Yes.
B. No.

8. Strongest backup evidence?
A. A file named backup exists.
B. A separate test restore succeeds and records are verified.

9. It works locally. Ready for customers?
A. Not necessarily; access, data, reliability and maintenance need review.
B. Yes.

10. Does a free course guarantee free tools?
A. Yes.
B. No; providers set their own prices and limits.

STOP AND RECORD YOUR ANSWERS

ANSWER KEY
1. B — bounded work is easier to finish and test. Lesson 1.
2. A — separate practice protects real records. Lesson 2.
3. B — reported success needs verification. Lesson 4.
4. B — reproducible symptoms make fixes easier. Lesson 4.
5. B — source history and business data need separate attention. Lesson 4.
6. A — findings need evaluation. Lesson 5.
7. B — actual authorization controls access. Lesson 5.
8. B — demonstrated recovery matters. Lesson 5.
9. A — a prototype needs further checks. Lesson 5.
10. B — the course is free; services may not be. Lesson 1.

YOUR NEXT STEP
8–10: review missed answers, then do the practical check.
5–7: revisit the linked lessons and retry.
0–4: return to lesson 1 and work through one exercise at a time.

PRACTICAL CHECK
Show your four-line brief, agreed plan, five workflow checks, source checkpoint and readiness note. Explain one feature you left out and one unresolved issue before real use. A quiz score does not prove an app is safe.

Mark done when you have reviewed the answers and completed the practical check.
